questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 takes the puck from YOU. What should you notice first?

options.text: Who has it now?
Can I pass the old way?
Did Navy2 score?

questions.explanation: Gold1 now has the puck, so YOU must notice the change before deciding what to do. YOU cannot keep passing as though the puck were still yours.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 moves to a new spot while YOU hold the puck. Which two players should YOU keep track of?

options.text: Gold1, who may block the way
Navy2 in the new spot
Only where Navy2 used to stand

questions.explanation: Check where Navy2 is now and where Gold1 is before choosing a pass. A teammate’s old spot may no longer be useful.

questions.prompt: Move YOU with the puck to try a different passing angle toward Navy2.
questions.explanation: Try a controlled move that leaves a clear path toward Navy2 while keeping Gold1 in view. The puck stays with YOU. This is one example to discuss, not the only place that can work.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 skates closer to YOU. Tell an adult what changed.
questions.explanation: A useful answer names Gold1 as closer pressure and Navy2 as a teammate to find. The next puck touch should follow that new picture.

questions.prompt: After YOU collect it, Navy2 asks for a pass. What helps before sending it?

options.text: Look to see if Navy2 is ready
Pass at once because you heard a call
Keep looking only at your stick

questions.explanation: A call helps you find Navy2. Look up and check that your partner is ready before passing.

questions.prompt: After the pickup, what helps a pass reach Navy2?

options.text: See where Navy2 is now
Look for Navy2’s ready stick
Aim where Navy2 stood before moving

questions.explanation: Find the partner and their ready stick. If Navy2 moves, the old spot may no longer be a useful target.

questions.prompt: Move Navy2 to give YOU a short pass after the pickup. Leave room between you.
questions.explanation: This brings Navy2 onto a shorter passing line from the pickup area. A different clear target can work if both players are ready.

questions.prompt: You touched the puck, but it slid away. Is your pickup finished? Tell a grown-up.
questions.explanation: Touching the puck once is different from controlling it. Find it again, approach under control, and keep it close enough for your next touch.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 covers your first angle, what should Navy2 see?

options.text: A different clear target or lane
YOU staying behind Gold1
A pass through the defender

questions.explanation: Gold1 removed the first window. A new angle or lane gives Navy2 a real choice if it is visible.

questions.prompt: After moving, what two players should YOU check?

options.text: Navy2, who is waiting for a pass
Gold1, who may have moved
A player outside the scene

questions.explanation: YOU have the puck, so YOU choose the next play. Navy2 is the teammate who could receive it, and Gold1 could change the way there. Only the players in this picture can be checked.

questions.prompt: Place YOU in a spot where the way to Navy2 stays open.
questions.explanation: This spot keeps the way to Navy2 open and is closer to your partner than the empty-side example. Gold1 is still ahead in the middle, so check the way again after any move. Other open spots can work; the test is whether the path to Navy2 stays clear.

questions.prompt: Imagine YOU pass to Navy2 and Navy2 now has the puck. How can you show you are ready for a return pass?
questions.explanation: This is a stated change: in the picture YOU still have the puck. After a pass, moving where Navy2 can see you and keeping your stick ready are ways to show it. Whether a return pass fits still depends on where Gold1 is.

questions.prompt: While YOU wait for your turn, what helps YOU look after the puck?

options.text: Keep it close to your stick
Leave it in the middle of the circle
Shoot it toward the boards

questions.explanation: YOU are carrying the puck while Navy2 uses the circle. Keeping it close means it is ready when your turn comes and it stays out of your partner’s space. A coach may instead ask players to set their pucks aside for a turn; sending it away can also mean chasing it later.

questions.prompt: Before leaving the boards for your turn, what should YOU check?

options.text: Where the coach asked you to go
Whether the way there is clear
Whether you can beat Navy2 to the spot

questions.explanation: Find the named practice spot and check your route. Getting there first is not the aim of this reset.

questions.prompt: For another waiting spot, move Navy2 outside the circle on its centre-ice side.
questions.explanation: This waiting spot stays outside the painted circle and gives the next player room. The coach can choose another clear waiting place.

questions.prompt: Can you skate across the painted circle line to reach the middle? What should you look for?
questions.explanation: The circle is paint on the ice, not a wall. You can cross it in this activity after checking the way is clear and it is your turn.

questions.prompt: You have stopped, but the puck slides away. What could YOU do while the coach is talking?

options.text: Listen and ask before going to get it
Follow the puck straight away
Ask Navy2 to race after it

questions.explanation: Stay with the stop-and-listen instruction. Ask for help collecting the puck rather than starting another chase.

questions.prompt: Before turning to listen, what helps YOU give Navy2 room?

options.text: Look where Navy2 is
Keep your stick in your own space
Move beside Navy2 without looking

questions.explanation: Notice your partner while you turn and leave room for both players and their sticks.

questions.prompt: The coach asks Navy2 to use more space for the next try. Move Navy2 farther from YOUR lane.
questions.explanation: This separates the two practice lanes. It is a new coach-directed setup, not permission to restart before the next signal.

questions.prompt: You did not hear what the coach said next. What could you say?
questions.explanation: Try “Can you say that again?” or “Can you show me?” Asking helps you know when and where to start the next try.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2’s pass slides a little behind YOU. What could YOU do?

options.text: Turn and skate to the puck under control
Wait for Navy2 to come and get it
Reach across without moving your feet

questions.explanation: Missing the first touch is normal in practice. Turning and going to the puck keeps the activity going. Reaching without moving your feet often puts you off balance, and waiting leaves the puck where it stopped. Nothing in this picture shows how hard or how fast a pass would be.

questions.prompt: Which two things can YOU see that help YOU get ready?

options.text: Navy2 has the puck
The ice between YOU and Navy2 is open
Which hand Navy2 shoots with

questions.explanation: The picture shows Navy2 with the puck and no player between the partners. The player artwork does not establish a reliable shooting-hand cue for this question.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a second waiting spot that keeps the ice to Navy2 open.
questions.explanation: No player stands between this spot and Navy2, and Navy2 would not have to turn far to see YOU. Gold1 is not part of this try, so the choice is about staying visible to your partner. Other open spots can work; the test is whether the ice between the partners stays clear.

questions.prompt: Gold1 is not in this try. What would change if Gold1 joined in?
questions.explanation: With nobody challenging, YOU can pick a waiting spot mainly for a clear view of Navy2. If someone joined in, YOU would also check where they are and whether the ice between the partners is still open. This picture does not show that change, so any answer about it is a discussion, not something the scene proves.

questions.prompt: It is YOUR turn near the navy net. Where should YOU look first?

options.text: At Gold1 and the puck
At the far end of the rink
At your own skates

questions.explanation: Gold1 has the puck near your net, so watch Gold1 and the puck. If Navy2 gains control, follow the puck to Navy2 and check what happens next. The play may still be near your net.

questions.prompt: Which two things tell YOU where the play is right now?

options.text: Gold1 has the puck
How close the puck is to the navy net
Who takes the next turn after YOU

questions.explanation: The puck owner and how close the puck is to your net tell YOU what is happening now. Who takes the next turn matters between turns, not during this one.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a spot in front of the navy net where you can still see the puck.
questions.explanation: From here YOU stay in front of the navy net and can still see Gold1 and the puck. It is one example spot, and where you stand changes as the puck moves. This is an activity suggestion, not goaltending technique.

questions.prompt: Why does everyone get a turn defending the goal?
questions.explanation: Sharing the turn lets every player practise many parts of the game instead of only one. Any answer in your own words is fine, and nothing here is scored.

questions.prompt: Gold1 moves into the way ahead. What could YOU look for behind your shoulder?

options.text: Navy2 and a clear way to pass
The same forward route again
The nearest goal only

questions.explanation: Navy2 is behind YOU. Looking there can reveal a different choice, but you still need a clear passing lane.

questions.prompt: What should YOU check before a pass back to Navy2?

options.text: Where Navy2’s stick is now
Whether Gold1 can reach the passing lane
Only which way YOUR skates point

questions.explanation: A teammate behind you can help if you locate the target and check the lane. Facing forward does not remove the option of a pass back.

questions.prompt: Move Navy2 to a new waiting place behind YOU, with room for a short pass.
questions.explanation: Navy2 stays behind the way YOU face and separate from YOUR spot. Several nearby places can give a different passing angle.

questions.prompt: Why might a short pass back to Navy2 help you go forward later?
questions.explanation: It can move the puck away from Gold1’s pressure and give your team another view of the space ahead. Passing back is useful when that lane is clear; you do not have to use it every time.

questions.prompt: Gold1 skates closer to Navy2. What could YOU do to stay useful?

options.text: Find open space where Navy2 could reach YOU with a pass
Skate straight at Navy2 to take the puck back
Stand still until someone calls your name

questions.explanation: Navy2 has the puck and Gold1 is the pressure. Open space gives Navy2 a choice. It only becomes a pass if the route from Navy2 to YOU stays clear.

questions.prompt: Which two things should YOU watch now that Navy2 has the puck?

options.text: Where Navy2 is on the ice
Where Gold1 is coming from
Where the puck was before the pass

questions.explanation: Your teammate and the pressure are the two cues that change what YOU do next. Where the puck used to be can be useful context, but checking Navy2 and Gold1 tells YOU what matters now.

questions.prompt: Place YOU in open space where Navy2 could pass to YOU, away from Gold1.
questions.explanation: From here YOU are on the opposite side from Gold1 with a short open route to the puck. It is one example spot; another open place can work, and a pass still depends on that route staying clear.

questions.prompt: Why does Navy2 need room after taking the pass?
questions.explanation: Standing too close takes away the space Navy2 needs to carry the puck, and it can bring Gold1 to both of you at once. Any answer in your own words is fine.

questions.prompt: Gold1 has the puck now. What is a good first thing for YOU to do?

options.text: Notice who has the puck and where Navy2 is
Wait for the coach to tell YOU what happened
Skate to where the pass was going

questions.explanation: The puck changed hands, so the old plan is finished. Noticing the new owner and where your teammate is gives YOU something useful to do next.

questions.prompt: Which two things are true in this picture?

options.text: Gold1 is the puck owner
The pass to Navy2 did not finish
YOU are the navy player closest to the puck

questions.explanation: The picture starts after the miss, with Gold1 holding the puck. Navy2 is actually the navy player nearer the puck, so the third choice does not match what YOU can see.

questions.prompt: Place YOU in open space where Navy2 can find YOU for the next try.
questions.explanation: This gives YOU room on the far side from Gold1 and a short open route to Navy2 for the next try. It is one example spot; another open place can work. The picture does not prove Navy2 has already looked at YOU.

questions.prompt: What does “another try” mean after a missed pass?
questions.explanation: It means noticing what is true now, that Gold1 has the puck and Navy2 does not, and then getting ready to help again. Repeating the old pass plan without looking ignores where Gold1 is. Any answer in your own words is fine.
